title: The die is cast
author: Suetonius

source_text: Tunc Caesar: "Eatur," inquit, "quo deorum ostenta et inimicorum iniquitas vocat. Iacta alea est," inquit.

translation: Then Caesar said, "Let us go where the signs of the gods and the injustice of our enemies are calling. The die has been cast," he said.
translation_note: Eātur is an impersonal passive ("let there be going"); "let us go" is the natural English. Iacta est is a perfect passive: the throw has already happened.

essay.t: The Rubicon was a small stream that marked the boundary between the province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy; when Caesar led his army across it in 49 BC, he began a civil war.
Which modern river it was is not settled: the Rubicone is the official identification, but other rivers have been proposed.

Suetonius describes Caesar halting at the river and telling those around him that they could still turn back, but that once they crossed the little bridge, everything would have to be settled by arms.
Then, he says, a man of unusual size and beauty appeared, playing a reed pipe, seized a trumpet from one of the trumpeters who had gathered, and crossed to the far bank sounding the call to battle.
Only after this omen does Caesar speak the words of our passage, so in Suetonius the decision is framed as an answer to the gods as much as to his enemies.
Notice the word order: Suetonius writes iacta alea est, not the alea iacta est that is usually quoted today.
Plutarch, writing in Greek, calls "let the die be cast" the phrase with which people usually launch into desperate ventures, and in his Life of Pompey he says Caesar called it out in Greek.
Appian also calls it a familiar phrase, in the form "The die is cast: so let it be!"
The same Greek words occur in a comedy by Menander quoted by Athenaeus, where a character uses them of a marriage that has been decided; whether Caesar had Menander in mind is only a guess.

So we cannot be sure whether Caesar spoke Latin or Greek, or whether he said anything at all: Suetonius was born about AD 69, more than a century later, and he used anecdotes without always testing them.
What the sources agree on is the meaning: a throw of the dice cannot be taken back, and the phrase still names a decision with no return.

questions.q: In Suetonius, what happens just before Caesar says "Iacta alea est"?
options: A figure seizes a trumpet and crosses the river sounding the call to battle

questions.q: According to Plutarch's Life of Pompey, in which language did Caesar call out the phrase?
